title: Signature Tag Lineage Registry
description: Signature edition: every encrypted tag records its lineage — who created it, under what authority, when it was last re-encrypted or rotated. Tags are accountable artifacts; orphaned or stale tags are flagged for review. This is a Signature original method.
method: Register (tag, creator, authority, rotation date); flag stale/orphaned tags; review quarterly.
usage: Register tags at creation; the registry is the audit trail for classification decisions.

demo.code: print('tag registry: 35 tags, 2 stale (rotation overdue) -> flagged')

title: Signature Attribute-based encryption (ABE)
description: Signature edition: ABE encrypts to a policy, not a person: 'decryptable by (doctor AND cardiology) OR (researcher AND trial-X)'. Ciphertext carries the access policy; keys carry attributes; decryption works iff attributes satisfy the policy — fine-grained access control enforced by math, not by a server.
method: Encrypt under a policy; issue attribute keys; decryption succeeds iff attributes satisfy the policy.
usage: Design the attribute universe carefully; revocation is the hard part — plan for it.

demo.code:
print('policy: (role=doctor AND dept=cardiology)')
print('key attributes {doctor, cardiology}: DECRYPTS; {nurse}: denied')

title: Signature Metadata minimization
description: Signature edition: The best encrypted metadata is no metadata: minimization asks what tags are truly needed and deletes the rest. Every tag is a liability (even encrypted, it leaks existence and size); the minimization review regularly prunes tags nobody uses.
method: Inventory all metadata; justify each tag's existence; delete unjustified tags; review quarterly.
usage: Default to fewer tags; each new tag needs a written justification.

demo.code:
print('metadata inventory: 47 tags')
print('review: 12 unjustified -> DELETED; 35 kept with reasons')

title: Signature Encrypted tagging for classification
description: Signature edition: Documents carry encrypted tags (classification level, project code) that only authorized classifiers can read or match. Routing and access decisions use the tags without exposing them to the infrastructure — the mailroom sorts sealed envelopes by their wax seals.
method: Encrypt tags with ABE or per-role keys; infrastructure matches ciphertext tags to routing rules; content stays sealed.
usage: Separate tag keys from content keys; rotate tag keys on role changes.

demo.code:
print('tag enc("top-secret") routable by mailroom (sees: project-X sealed)')
print('content key: separate, held by cleared analysts only')

title: Signature Traffic-analysis resistance
description: Signature edition: Even encrypted tags leak via traffic analysis: message sizes, timing, frequencies. Resistance means padding to uniform sizes, batching and mixing sends, and cover traffic — making the observable pattern reveal nothing. The metadata's metadata needs protection too.
method: Pad to fixed sizes; batch sends; add cover traffic; randomize timing within bounds.
usage: Apply where the adversary watches the network; measure the overhead honestly.

demo.code:
print('all messages padded to 4KB, sent in 5-min batches')
print('observer sees: uniform blobs on schedule (nothing else)')

title: Signature Zero-knowledge tag proofs
description: Signature edition: Prove a tag satisfies a policy without revealing the tag: 'this document is releasable to role X' proved in zero knowledge. The verifier learns the authorization decision, not the classification details — need-to-know enforced cryptographically.
method: Commit to the tag; prove the policy predicate in ZK; the verifier checks the proof, learns only the decision.
usage: Use for cross-domain authorization where tag values are themselves sensitive.

demo.code:
print('prove: clearance(tag) >= required (ZK)')
print('verifier: AUTHORIZED (tag value unseen)')

title: Signature Order-preserving encryption
description: Signature edition: OPE preserves order: enc(a) < enc(b) iff a < b, enabling range queries on encrypted data. It leaks order (inherently), so modern guidance prefers it only where range queries are essential and the leakage is modeled — again CryptDB's approach with explicit leakage analysis.
method: Encrypt with an order-preserving scheme; B-tree indexes work on ciphertext; analyze and document order leakage.
usage: Use only for required range queries; model the leakage; consider alternatives (ORAM, trusted hardware).

demo.code:
print('enc(25) < enc(40): range query [20,50] works on ciphertext')
print('leakage: order visible (accepted for this column, documented)')

title: Signature Format-preserving encryption
description: Signature edition: FPE encrypts while keeping the format: a 16-digit card number encrypts to another 16-digit number, so legacy databases and validations keep working. NIST's FF1/FF3 standardize it — the pragmatic way to encrypt fields in systems that can't change shape.
method: Encrypt with FF1/FF3 over the field's alphabet; ciphertext matches the format; legacy code works unchanged.
usage: Use for fixed-format PII in legacy systems; remember FPE doesn't hide the format itself.

demo.code:
print('card 4111-1111-1111-1111 -> FPE -> 8024-7731-0092-4451')
print('still 16 digits: passes legacy validation, value hidden')

title: Signature Deterministic encryption for equality
description: Signature edition: Deterministic encryption (same plaintext -> same ciphertext) enables equality queries on encrypted columns: 'find all records with this encrypted SSN'. It leaks equality patterns, so it's for low-sensitivity equality matching with the tradeoff stated explicitly — CryptDB's onion layers work this way.
method: Encrypt deterministically (e.g., AES-SIV); the database indexes ciphertext; equality queries work; document the leakage.
usage: Use only where equality queries are required; state the leakage; prefer randomized encryption elsewhere.

demo.code:
print('enc(ssn) deterministic -> index lookup works')
print('leakage: equal SSNs visible as equal ciphertexts (documented)')
